meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The world is a stage, but the play is badly cast'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified as genuine Wilde — the closing line of the 'Actors are so fortunate' passage in 'Lord Arthur Savile's Crime' (1887).

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: It is the closing epigram of a passage in Chapter I of Wilde’s short story “Lord Arthur Savile’s Crime” (first published in The Court and Society Review, 1887; collected 1891). The exact wording—“but the play is badly cast”—is confirmed in the original text.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Lord Arthur Savile’s Crime and Other Stories (1891)

source.excerpt: Actors are so fortunate. They can choose whether they will appear in tragedy or in comedy, whether they will suffer or make merry, laugh or shed tears. But in real life it is different. Most men and women are forced to perform parts for which they have no qualifications. Our Guildensterns play Hamlet for us, and our Hamlets have to jest like Prince Hal. The world is a stage, but the play is badly cast.
trail: The exact epigram closes the “Actors are so fortunate…” passage in Chapter I of Lord Arthur Savile’s Crime ↗.
The story first appeared in The Court and Society Review in 1887 and was collected in 1891, per Wikipedia ↗.
Quote databases reproduce the full passage under Wilde’s name, e.g. AZQuotes ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular one-liner drops the whole passage that sets it up
source.excerptNote: In the story the lines are narration—Wilde voicing Lord Arthur’s dark musings after a palm-reader’s alarming reading leaves him sensing a doom that is, moments later, spelled out as a murder he is fated to commit.

sourceLink.text: Read the full text at Project Gutenberg

source.rightsNote: Wilde died in 1900 and the text dates to 1887, so the quote is firmly in the public domain.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: About Oscar Wilde
author.bio: Oscar Wilde (1854–1900) was an Irish poet, dramatist and aphorist, celebrated for plays such as The Importance of Being Earnest and his sole novel The Picture of Dorian Gray. “Lord Arthur Savile’s Crime,” a semi-comic tale of fate and murder, was one of his earliest published stories. Its inversion of Shakespeare’s “All the world’s a stage” is characteristic Wilde: a familiar line turned inside out for wit.

misattribution.heading: Attribution notes
misattribution.intro: The epigram is genuinely Wilde’s, but it circulates in a softened form and is occasionally credited to the wrong pen.

items.why: Wilde wrote “but the play is badly cast” in Chapter I; the smoother “and” version spread through Goodreads and quote sites but is not the original text ↗.
Because the line deliberately riffs on Shakespeare’s “All the world’s a stage” (As You Like It), some assume the whole epigram is the Bard’s—but it appears in Wilde’s own story ↗, not in Shakespeare.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: this is verified Wilde—the closing line of the “Actors are so fortunate…” passage in Lord Arthur Savile’s Crime ↗ (1887).

context.heading: Why it lands
lead: The barb works because it hijacks the most famous stage metaphor in English. Shakespeare’s Jaques declares that “All the world’s a stage, / And all the men and women merely players”; Wilde keeps the conceit but adds a theatre critic’s verdict—the casting is all wrong. Guildensterns are handed Hamlet; Hamlets are stuck clowning like Prince Hal.
In context it is not a throwaway witticism but a flash of fatalism: Lord Arthur, told he is destined to kill, broods that people are forced into roles they were never suited to play.
context.pull: Our Guildensterns play Hamlet for us, and our Hamlets have to jest like Prince Hal.
